title: Elena Rybakina becomes world No. 1 for first time after U.S. Open win over Zheng Qinwen
content:
NEW YORK — Women’s tennis has a new world No. 1.

Elena Rybakina took over the top spot from Aryna Sabalenka on Wednesday at the U.S. Open with a quarterfinal win over China’s Zheng Qinwen, 3-6, 6-1, 6-4. It is her first time at the summit of women’s tennis.

Born in Moscow but representing Kazakhstan, Rybakina, 27, has been a top-five player for years but inched towards tennis’s apex earlier this season after winning the Australian Open to claim her second Grand Slam title. She won the Stuttgart Tennis Grand Prix on clay in April and owns the second-most wins on the WTA tour this year with 47, following Jessica Pegula’s 50.

Rybakina was a mostly steady force in a season of relative shakiness at the top of the tour’s leaderboard.

After she won the year’s first Grand Slam in January, the major-title winners club admitted two new members as the old — well, older — guard looked on. Mirra Andreeva won the French Open at 19 and Linda Nosková won Wimbledon at 21.

If Sabalenka does not win the U.S. Open, she will log her first year since 2022 without a Grand Slam title. Coco Gauff, who faces Andreeva in the last women’s quarterfinal Wednesday, could win her third major championship. World No. 3 Jessica Pegula is still searching for her first Grand Slam title after spending years as one of the most consistent players at the top of the game. Iga Świątek, the most decorated champion in the group with six majors, is headed toward the end of a trying year that included a coaching change, lost to Zheng in the U.S. Open’s fourth round.

Sabalenka, Gauff, Świątek and Rybakina all had significant periods of instability in 2026. But none was as apparent as Sabalenka’s, both because of how demonstrative she is and because of how untouchable she seemed as the top player just months ago.

She spent 99 weeks as the world No. 1 after taking over from Świątek in surprising fashion in 2024.

After losing the Australian Open final against Rybakina in January, Sabalenka won their rematch in the Indian Wells final and beat Coco Gauff in the Miami Open final in March.

Then, the trouble began.

She lost to then-world No. 32 Hailey Baptiste on clay in the quarterfinals of the Madrid Open and the wheels came off after that. Sabalenka made just two quarterfinals in her next six events. She lost two matches in which she lost at least a set 6-0 — one in a train wreck of a quarterfinal loss to Diana Schnaider at the French Open, another to Jessica Pegula at the Berlin Open on grass.

Sabalenka faces Pegula in one U.S. Open semifinal, while Rybakina will play either Gauff or Andreeva in the other.

She came back to beat Zheng in classic Rybakina fashion — by asserting her power game on a player who couldn’t keep up. Zheng’s game is by no means lacking fire, but the former Olympic champion came through qualifying to reach the quarterfinals after her ranking dipped as she’s been managing a chronic elbow injury.

After coming back from trailing 5-0 in a set in two different matches in New York, Zheng’s energy finally dipped in the second set against Rybakina. She struggled with her first serve throughout the match, but serving at 4-4, in the third set she double-faulted to give Rybakina the chance to serve out the match.

Her opponent’s misstep was a gift. Just as she has all season, Rybakina capitalized on the opportunity.
